title: Baseline cognitive impairment predicts cerebrovascular events in stroke-free chinese adults
Allele-specific GNB3 modulation of APOE ε4 memory effects
abstract: Abstract Modern environmental improvements have extended average lifespan, leading to increased prevalence of neurodegenerative diseases such as dementia. While memory decline is a natural physiological process of aging, numerous studies have demonstrated that certain genotypes increase the risk of cognitive decline and dementia. The apolipoprotein E ( APOE ) ε4 allele is a well-established risk factor for Alzheimer’s disease (AD), the primary cause of dementia. APOE ε4 carriers not only have significantly elevated AD risk but also exhibit poorer cognitive performance and episodic memory decline. However, APOE ε4 alone inadequately predicts AD; its predictive power is limited by incomplete penetrance and polygenic interactions. Genome-wide association studies identify guanine nucleotide-binding protein beta polypeptide 3 ( GNB3 ), a G-protein β subunit hub in APOE ε4-specific co-expression networks, but evidence linking GNB3 C825T to cognition or its interaction with APOE ε4 remains absent. In this study, we genotyped APOE and GNB3 C825T (rs5443) in 369 cognitively healthy adults at a healthy aging exhibition in Taiwan and assessed short-term memory performance. APOE ε4 carriers showed poorer short-term memory performance compared with non-carriers. While GNB3 genotype alone was not associated with memory performance, subgroup analyses suggested a trend toward poorer performance among APOE ε4 carriers with the GNB3 T allele (OR = 2.08, p = 0.08). However, formal interaction analysis did not demonstrate a statistically significant interaction effect. These findings suggest a potential association between APOE ε4 and short-term memory performance and indicate that GNB3 genotype may influence this relationship.

title: Peripheral serum biomarkers and MRI-derived accelerated brain aging: a cross-sectional study using deep learning-based brain age estimation
abstract: Abstract Brain age gap is an emerging neuroimaging marker that captures interindividual variation in brain structural aging. Identifying accessible peripheral biomarkers associated with accelerated brain aging may improve early risk recognition and provide insight into systemic biological processes linked to brain health. This study investigated the associations between routine serum laboratory biomarkers and MRI-derived brain age gap in a health examination cohort. We included 852 participants with available structural MRI and routine laboratory data. Brain age was estimated from structural MRI using a deep learning model, and corrected brain age gap (CorrectedBAG) was derived to reduce age-related prediction bias. We evaluated 25 serum laboratory biomarkers spanning metabolic, immune-inflammatory, hepatic, renal, and bone/nutrition-related domains. Multivariable linear regression was used to examine associations with CorrectedBAG, and restricted cubic spline models were applied to assess potential nonlinear dose-response relationships. Binary logistic regression was further used to evaluate accelerated brain aging defined by brain age gap thresholds. Among the 25 biomarkers examined, serum alkaline phosphatase (ALP) and neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (NLR) showed independent positive associations with CorrectedBAG. Higher ALP was associated with greater CorrectedBAG (β = 0.4073, 95% CI 0.1534–0.6613; P = 0.0017), as was higher NLR (β = 0.2558, 95% CI 0.0164–0.4952; P = 0.0365). In logistic regression analyses, ALP was consistently associated with greater odds of accelerated brain aging defined as BAG > 0 years (OR = 1.011, 95% CI 1.003–1.019; P = 0.010) and BAG > 3 years (OR = 1.013, 95% CI 1.004–1.023; P = 0.006). NLR was also associated with BAG > 3 years (OR = 1.333; P = 0.005). Restricted cubic spline analyses supported approximately linear associations of ALP and NLR with CorrectedBAG. In this Asian health examination cohort, higher serum ALP and NLR were associated with greater MRI-derived brain age gap. These findings suggest that routinely available serum biomarkers may capture peripheral biological processes related to accelerated brain structural aging. Further studies are warranted to clarify the temporal relationships and biological pathways underlying these associations.

title: Development and exploratory feasibility of a social cognitive theory-based family intergenerational support intervention for rural older adults with cognitive impairment
abstract: Guided by Social Cognitive Theory (SCT) as the theoretical framework and family-based intergenerational support as the implementation pathway, this study developed a family-based intergenerational support intervention for rural older adults with cognitive impairment. An exploratory feasibility pilot study was subsequently conducted. It described recruitment and retention, completion of assessment procedures, family participation, and implementation challenges. The findings were used to inform further protocol refinement and future feasibility research. The intervention was developed based on the core mechanisms of Social Cognitive Theory, including self-efficacy, observational learning, behavioral reinforcement, and environmental support, through a literature review, research team discussions, and two rounds of Delphi expert consultation. The intervention comprised three modules: self-management, psychological intervention, and cognitive training. Representative activities included walking, looking at old photographs, everyday-life calculation tasks, and memory training. Under the guidance of healthcare professionals, younger-generation family members were intended to support patients’ participation in the planned activities through companionship, reminders, demonstrations, joint activities, and feedback recording. From June to July 2026, eight rural older adults with cognitive impairment admitted to Fuyang Third People’s Hospital were recruited using purposive sampling. Each participant was enrolled together with one younger-generation family member who was primarily involved in their care, and all dyads took part in a 2-week pilot study. Two nurses documented patient participation, available information on task implementation, and family-member feedback through WeChat communication, observations during intervention delivery, and follow-up. A researcher-developed four-item family feedback form was used to assess overall satisfaction, understanding and implementation of the intervention content, willingness to participate in future research, and satisfaction with the research staff’s service attitude. Open-ended questions were used to collect family-reported patient activity preferences and suggestions for intervention refinement. The Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA), 15-item Geriatric Depression Scale (GDS-15), and Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI) were administered to document completion of the assessment procedures, and the data were analyzed descriptively. The effective response rates of the two rounds of expert consultation were 100.0% and 94.4%, respectively, and the coefficients of expert authority were 0.79 and 0.85, respectively. In the second round, the mean importance scores of items at all levels ranged from 4.53 to 4.94, and the mean operability scores of tertiary-level items ranged from 4.18 to 4.82. Kendall’s coefficients of concordance for the importance ratings of items at all levels and the operability ratings of tertiary-level items were 0.591 and 0.617, respectively (both P < 0.001). After two rounds of expert consultation, a modular pilot intervention protocol was developed, consisting of 3 primary items, 12 secondary items, and 34 tertiary items. During the recruitment phase, 10 eligible individuals were screened, of whom 8 were enrolled, resulting in an enrollment rate of 80.0%. All 8 enrolled participants remained in the 2-week pilot study period and completed pre- and post-pilot assessments, yielding a retention rate and assessment completion rate of 100.0%. All 8 younger-generation family members participated in the family support process during the 2-week pilot study and primarily provided assistance through companionship, reminders, task demonstrations, and process documentation. In the family feedback questionnaire, the mean scores for the four items—research staff attitude, overall satisfaction, understanding and implementation of intervention content, and willingness to participate in future studies—were 4.50 ± 0.53, 4.00 ± 0.53, 3.63 ± 0.52, and 3.88 ± 0.83, respectively. Feedback from implementing nurses indicated that the intervention protocol was characterized by modular design, integration of tasks into daily life, and family involvement. However, several implementation challenges were identified, including insufficient guidance strategies for family members, difficulties in understanding some tasks, and limited availability of family time. Based on pilot feedback, the research team refined the implementation methods, task difficulty, scheduling arrangements, and process documentation procedures for selected tertiary items while maintaining the overall intervention framework and primary intervention components unchanged. This study developed a preliminary family-based intergenerational support intervention for rural older adults with cognitive impairment and conducted an exploratory feasibility pilot study. The pilot study described recruitment and retention, completion of assessment procedures, family participation, and implementation-related challenges. Feedback from younger-generation family members and observations by implementing nurses indicated that further refinement is needed regarding task comprehension, family guidance strategies, and time arrangements. These findings only reflect the specific process indicators and implementation experiences observed in this sample and cannot establish the overall feasibility of the intervention, patient acceptability, or intervention effectiveness. The refined intervention protocol requires further examination in larger samples, diverse family contexts, and studies incorporating standardized process evaluations.

title: FDG PET evidence suggests the left insula may be a hub for cognitive reserve in mild cognitive impairment
abstract: Cognitive reserve (CR) refers to the ability to cope with the detrimental effects of ageing or brain pathology on cognition. Individuals with higher CR may maintain cognitive performance despite a greater burden of underlying brain pathology. This study aimed to characterize cerebral metabolic patterns associated with CR in subjects with amnestic mild cognitive impairment (aMCI) using [18]F-FDG PET/CT, and to identify brain regions associated with higher CR. Sixty-three subjects with aMCI were included in this cross-sectional study. Based on the Cognitive Reserve Index questionnaire (CRIq), 29 participants were classified as having high CR (HCR) and 34 as having low CR (LCR). Brain [18]F-FDG PET/CT scans were obtained in all participants and compared with those of 19 cognitively healthy subjects (HS). Voxel-wise analyses and volume-of-interest analyses were performed to assess regional metabolic differences, and multivariable regression models evaluated the association between CRIq and insular metabolism after adjustment for age and sex. Both HCR and LCR groups exhibited the characteristic temporo-parietal pattern of Alzheimer’s disease-related hypometabolism compared with HS. Direct voxel-wise comparison between HCR and LCR identified a significant difference in the left anterior insula, where metabolism was relatively preserved in HCR. Left insular metabolism was positively associated with CRIq score independently of age and sex. These findings suggest that relatively preserved left insular metabolism is associated with higher CR in aMCI and identify the left anterior insula as a candidate neural substrate of CR. Future longitudinal studies will be important to confirm these findings and clarify the mechanisms possibly linking left insular metabolism to CR.

title: Validity and reliability study of the Turkish version of the Bipolar recovery questionnaire in Bipolar affective disorder
abstract: Abstract The aim of this study was to assess the validity and reliability of the Turkish versions of the Bipolar Recovery Questionnaire (BRQ) and to examine the clinical variables associated with personal recovery. This was a single-center cross-sectional study. Outpatients with the diagnosis of Bipolar I Disorder (BD I) were included in the study. The BRQ was translated from English into Turkish and back-translated into English. Internal consistency was assessed using Cronbach’s alpha, corrected item-total correlations, and Cronbach’s alpha if item deleted. Structured Clinical Interview for DSM-5,Clinical Version (SCID-5/CV), administered by the clinician, was used to confirm the diagnosis BD I. Subjective Recovery Assessment Scale (SubRAS), Personal and Social Performance Scale (PSP) and Global Assessment of Functioning (GAF) were used to examine convergent validity. The clinician-administered Hamilton Depression Rating Scale (HAM-D) and Young Mania Rating Scale (YMRS) were used to evaluate symptom severity in patients. Multivariable regression analysis was performed to evaluate the clinical variables associated with BRQ total scores. Cronbach’s alpha coefficient for BRQ was 0.888 and showed very good internal consistency. Corrected item-total score correlation coefficients ranged from − 0.114 to 0.742. Total BRQ score had moderate positive correlations with PSP (ρ = 0.432 , p < 0.001) and SubRAS (ρ = 0.383, p < 0.001), a weak positive correlation with GAF (ρ = 0.304 , p = 0.004), and a weak negative correlation with the HAM-D total score (ρ = -0.301 , p = 0.004). A weak positive correlation was observed between the total score of BRQ and the total duration of education (ρ = 0.265 , p = 0.012). Multivariable regression analysis showed that having a university degree was associated with higher BRQ scores compared with the reference education category. The present study provides preliminary evidence supporting the reliability and validity of the Turkish version of the BRQ for assessing personal recovery in individuals with BD I.

title: Psychological distress and sleep quality related to cognitive function in older adults with cognitive impairment
abstract: Abstract This study aimed to examine the associations between cognitive function, psychological distress, and sleep quality in older adults with cognitive impairment (CI). A cross-sectional analytical study was conducted in 129 older adults with CI. Cognitive functioning was assessed using standardized neuropsychological instrument, including the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA), together with complementary cognitive tests. Psychological distress was evaluated through anxiety, depression, and perceived stress measures, while sleep quality was assessed using the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI). The results showed the coexistence of cognitive impairment, moderate levels of psychological distress, and poor sleep quality in the sample. Significant correlations were observed between sleep quality and cognitive functioning, indicating that poorer sleep quality was associated with lower cognitive performance. Psychological distress variables were also significantly related to cognitive functioning and sleep quality. Multiple regression analyses indicated that global cognitive performance was significantly associated with sleep quality, perceived stress, and anxiety levels. These findings highlight the simultaneous association and potential interaction between sleep quality, psychological distress, and cognitive functioning in older adults with cognitive impairment and underscore the importance of considering these factors together when assessing cognitive health in aging populations.

title: Changes in mental health literacy and perceived psychological safety following a retired athlete–led, team-embedded education session in sport
abstract: Athletes experience mental health difficulties at rates comparable to or exceeding those of the general population, yet disclosure and help-seeking are often constrained by stigma and performance-oriented norms. This study evaluated a brief, retired-athlete–led, team-embedded mental health literacy (MHL) session and examined changes in MHL, perceived psychological safety, and help-seeking intention among athletes from two Japanese competitive sport teams in the women’s category. Thirty-four athletes (badminton, volleyball) attended a 90-min session integrating psychoeducation and facilitated team dialogue delivered by retired athletes who had completed facilitator training in mental health literacy. Using a single-group pre–post–2-month follow-up design, outcomes were assessed at baseline, immediately post-session, and follow-up. Mixed-effects models estimated change over time, with exploratory stratification by baseline psychological strain measured with the Athlete Psychological Strain Questionnaire (APSQ). MHL improved from baseline to post-session and remained higher at follow-up (standardised mean changes of 0.72 and 0.65, respectively). Perceived psychological safety also increased and was maintained (0.65 and 0.59). Exploratory subgroup estimates varied by baseline strain, although time × strain-group interactions were not statistically significant. The proportion endorsing likely/very likely help-seeking increased descriptively (41%, 53%, 50%) but showed no clear time effects. These preliminary findings support further controlled and implementation-oriented evaluation of retired-athlete–led delivery and downstream help-seeking behaviour.

title: Precision stratification of risk for suicidal behavior in people with bipolar depression
abstract: Patients with bipolar depression are at the highest risk for suicidal behavior, comprising ~ 10% of all deaths. In the critical period preceding attempts, most are not in contact with mental health professionals to effect anti-suicidal strategies. There is an urgent need for decision support tools to help nonspecialist providers identify those at elevated risk to facilitate prevention. However, we lack robust, performant predictive models to form the core of such tools. Here, we build a high-precision predictive model of 30-day risk for suicidal behavior using unique electronic health record data from > 220,000 patients with bipolar depression. We show that optimized machine learning approaches offer very strong clinical utility, delivering high Standardized Net Benefit in the context of near-perfect calibration and smooth, threshold-robust decision curves. Our results break the longstanding performance ceiling in suicide risk prediction and highlight the importance of training models for clinical utility as well as discriminative skill.

title: Efficient Alzheimer’s disease classification with robust rank pooling
abstract: Alzheimer’s disease (AD) classification utilizing 3D Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) on brain MRI poses significant challenges, including high computational overhead, the scarcity of large-scale training data, and the inherent difficulty in capturing subtle pathological features. Existing 3D-to-2D compression methods simplify the data but suffer from critical information loss. We propose Robust Rank Pooling (RRP), a novel compression technique that employs a sliding window strategy to transform a 3D MRI volume into multiple 2D dynamic images. This approach effectively mitigates information loss by preserving robust structural features across different brain sections. We utilize these generated images to train an efficient, pre-trained 2D CNN architecture, which incorporates a model ensemble method to further enhance performance. The proposed method is validated on two T2-FLAIR MRI benchmarks, ADNI and BICWALZS. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach significantly outperforms existing methods. Compared to the previous method, our model achieves improvements of approximately 2.3% in accuracy and 4.4% in Area Under the Curve (AUC). Relative to a standard 3D network, our method improves accuracy by 13.2% while demonstrating a 4.1 \(\times \) and 2.1 \(\times \) speedups in model inference and total processing time, respectively. Furthermore, qualitative analysis confirms that our model focuses on clinically relevant biomarkers, consequently offering a computationally efficient and effective solution for Alzheimer’s disease classification.

title: Skin carotenoid levels are associated with blood amyloid-beta 42/40 ratios in healthy individuals under 60 years of age
abstract: Dementia prevalence is increasing worldwide, with Alzheimer’s disease (AD) being the most common type. Amyloid-beta (Aβ) aggregation is an early pathological event in AD. Although carotenoids have been shown in vitro to inhibit Aβ aggregation through antioxidant and anti-inflammatory effects, human evidence remains limited. Recently, blood-based biomarkers such as Aβ42/40 ratios, phosphorylated tau (p-tau181, p-tau217), and neurofilament light chain (NfL) have enabled assessment of AD-related pathology. We analyzed 770 participants from the 2024 Iwaki Health Promotion Project in Japan. The associations between circulating carotenoid levels (skin and blood) and blood AD-related biomarkers were examined using adjusted linear and nonlinear regression models in a cross-sectional design. Among participants under 60 years, those in the highest quartile of skin carotenoid levels had significantly higher Aβ42/40 ratios than those in the lowest quartile (β = 0.0024, 95% CI: 0.0003–0.0046). The magnitude of the association was comparable to the cross-sectional difference in Aβ42/40 ratio observed across approximately 4–8 years of age. Among the blood carotenoids measured, lutein and α-carotene were positively associated with Aβ42/40 ratios. In summary, higher circulating carotenoid levels were associated with more favorable Aβ profiles in individuals under 60 years.

title: Neuropsychiatric symptom clusters across the cognitive impairment spectrum in advanced age: a data-driven analysis integrating AD biomarker and clinical profiling
abstract: Abstract Neuropsychiatric symptoms (NPS) are among the most common manifestations of cognitive impairment, yet their heterogeneity complicates understanding of how they relate to Alzheimer’s disease (AD) pathology. While individual NPS have been linked to AD biomarker burden, the interplay between co-occurring neuropsychiatric profiles and AD biomarkers in shaping cognitive and functional outcomes remains insufficiently understood. This study used data-driven clustering to identify NPS clusters in 300 individuals (156 mild cognitive impairment, 112 AD dementia, 32 non-AD dementia) using the 12 domains of Neuropsychiatric Inventory. K-means clustering identified three clusters: Minimal/No NPS (55.7%), Apathy-Behavioral Dysregulation (17.7%), and Depression-Anxiety/Affective (26.7%). Clusters differed significantly in age, sex, education, cognitive status, and diagnostic composition (all p < .05). The Apathy-Behavioral cluster showed advanced cognitive impairment and AD/non-AD dementia predominance, whereas the Depression-Anxiety cluster showed preserved cognition, female predominance, and highest vascular risk factor prevalence. Measured AD pathology (plasma pTau217, CSF amyloid and tau) did not differ across clusters, whereas APOE ε4 carriership was higher in the two symptomatic clusters (both 44.4% vs. 26.0%; p = .032), an association that did not persist after multivariable adjustment. Hierarchical regression revealed five of eight biomarker-outcome associations were largely independent of NPS clusters (change < 10%), with exceptions involving functional outcome: pTau217 (11.4%), tau (17.7%), and APOE ε4 (29.6%). Findings are consistent with a parallel-pathway hypothesis: measured AD pathology and NPS clusters showed largely independent associations with cognition, with only partial overlap in their associations with functional status.

title: Efficient deep learning models for early Alzheimer’s disease diagnosis
abstract: Abstract Alzheimer’s Disease (AD) is a progressive neurological disorder that impairs cognitive functions, severely affecting patients’ quality of life. Thus, early and accurate diagnosis is essential to provide a chance for treatment. This paper proposes two deep learning (DL) models to enable automated diagnosis of medical images. The first model is a hybrid of a convolutional neural network and bidirectional long short-term memory (CNN-BiLSTM) for classification of AD, and the second model is a U-Net for a segmentation task. The CNN-BiLSTM is applied to an overall dataset that consists of 6400 magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) images, while the U-Net is evaluated on a dataset that contains hippocampus regions that are isolated from the MRI images with manually labelled ground truth masks. The CNN-BiLSTM is implemented from scratch to detect four classes of AD: Non-Demented (ND), Mild Demented (MD), Moderate Demented (MOD), and Very Mild Demented (VMD). To tackle the issue of imbalanced classes in the dataset, data augmentation methods are employed to balance the dataset. The proposed CNN-BiLSTM model incorporates a Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping (Grad-CAM) processing technique to offer visual interpretations for its predictions. The Grad-CAM highlights the most relevant regions in MRI images that influence the model’s decisions and offers interpretability. Also, three explainable AI (XAI) techniques are applied to interpret the decision of the CNN-BiLSTM in the classification: Grad-CAM++, integrated gradient, and saliency map. The efficiency of the U-Net is assessed using two measurements: Dice Score and Intersection over Union (IoU). The proposed U-Net model achieved a Dice score of 92% and a mean IoU of 86%, which indicates high segmentation accuracy, while the CNN-BiLSTM achieves superior efficiency, with a testing accuracy of 99% and a testing loss rate of 0.0408. Also, the CNN-BiLSTM is measured by Precision, Recall, and F1-score metrics, all reaching 99%. The CNN-BiLSTM attains areas under the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves of 100%. These results underscore the potential of the proposed CNN-BiLSTM and U-Net integration to enhance the accuracy and reliability for diagnosing AD.

title: Mitochondrial and inflammatory markers as promising tools to enrich the diagnosis of schizophrenia and bipolar disorder
abstract: Mitochondrial dysfunction and low-grade inflammation have both been implicated in major mood and psychotic disorders, yet their interplay and association with specific symptom profiles and potential as diagnostic biomarkers remain unclear. We quantified mitochondrial markers including mitochondrial DNA copy number (mtDNA-cn), lactate, and circulating cell-free mitochondrial DNA (ccf-mtDNA) alongside immune markers in 934 individuals from the French I-GIVE cohort, including patients with schizophrenia (SCZ), bipolar disorder (BD), and healthy controls (HC). Both SCZ and BD were associated with increased lactate levels and with decreased mtDNA-cn during acute episodes. Mitochondrial markers correlated with inflammatory markers and clinical outcomes. Several inflammatory markers, including IL-1β, IL-6, IL-10, IL-13, IL-16, IL-17, TNF-α, and CRP, were also elevated in patients compared to controls. Models combining mitochondrial and inflammatory markers discriminated patients from controls with high accuracy and moderately distinguished SCZ from BD, while showing more limited performance for global functioning and disease onset. These findings support a contribution of mitochondrial and inflammatory alterations to the biological profile of severe psychiatric disorders. If replicated, such potential biomarkers may help refine diagnostic stratification and improve the characterization of clinical profiles.

title: Multi-class Alzheimer’s disease classification using VGG19 transfer learning with hybrid Harris Hawks Optimization and random forest
abstract: Abstract Accurate cognition-state classification of Alzheimer’s disease (AD), Mild Cognitive Impairment (MCI), and Cognitively Normal (CN) is essential for early evaluation of the disease. Existing deep-learning approaches often retain redundant features, depend on dataset-specific configurations, and provide limited methodological optimization. This study proposes a transfer-learning-based MRI classification framework integrating spatial and intensity normalization, histogram equalization, double bilateral filtering, VGG19-based deep feature extraction, Harris Hawks Optimization with Simulated Annealing (HHO-SA) for feature selection, and Random Forest (RF) classification. The framework was implemented using Python and PyTorch and evaluated on the ADNI1 Complete 1Yr 1.5T dataset, containing 2,294 MRI observations from 639 subjects. Subject-level partitioning was employed to minimize data leakage. The proposed framework achieved 98.70% accuracy, 98.55% macro-precision, 98.93% macro-recall, 99.28% macro-specificity, 98.73% macro-F1, and 99.40% macro-ROC-AUC. Compared with the strongest reported benchmark accuracy of 98.20%, this study developed into 0.50%. The findings demonstrate effective retrospective three-class MRI classification and provide a reproducible computational framework for AD research.

title: Seizure quality in bilateral electroconvulsive therapy: the influence of hyperventilation, electrode placement, and anesthesia
abstract: Abstract Electroconvulsive therapy (ECT) is an effective psychiatric treatment and relies on an iatrogenically induced, generalized seizure. Seizure quality scores have been developed to predict treatment outcomes of ECT. Its intensity can be governed by various parameters like electrode placement, anesthesia, and the systemic levels of CO₂. The aim of this retrospective study was to investigate whether reducing end-tidal CO₂ (etCO₂) through hyperventilation prior to ECT seizure would improve seizure quality score considering electrode placement and anesthetic agent. Case notes from 2023 were reviewed and seizure quality scores, pre-seizure etCO₂, electrode placement, and anesthetic agent were obtained. The resulting 732 ECTs from 68 patients were analyzed. Lower etCO₂ and its interaction with main anesthetic agent and different bilateral electrode placement were not significantly associated with improved seizure quality overall. Higher age was associated with a decrease in seizure quality (β = -0.03, SE = 0.01, z = − 5.58, p < .001). Post-hoc power analysis indicated sample sizes of at least 400 patients to detect isolated etCO 2 effects. Seizure quality should be understood as a complex interplay of technical, neurophysiological, and patient-related factors. Large and standardized multicenter studies are needed to explore the influence of treatment protocols on seizure quality.

title: A cell-based multivariate blood test (iCAP) for early detection of Alzheimer’s disease capturing non-amyloid-β biology
abstract: Abstract The indicator cell assay platform (iCAP) is a blood-based diagnostic approach that uses standardized cells as biosensors to transduce complex circulating signals into cell-based gene-expression profiles for multivariate disease classification. We developed an iCAP for early detection of Alzheimer’s disease (AD-iCAP) by incubating plasma from patients with early-stage AD (mild cognitive impairment or mild dementia) and non-affected controls with standardized neurons and training classifiers on transcriptomic responses. Modeling features were restricted to a predefined 84-gene panel derived independently by analyzing 5xFAD mouse plasma in the AD-iCAP. In this exploratory study, a model was trained and tested using 191 retrospectively collected human plasma samples across three cohorts. The classifier achieved AUC = 0.64 (95% CI 0.51–0.78) in an external validation set during model development (n = 82) and AUC = 0.77 (95% CI 0.57–0.96) in a blind test set (n = 23). The multivariate model incorporated 5 genes including AKT3 , GPR50 , PALLD , RGMA , and PCDH10 , implicated in AD, neuronal signaling and/or cytoskeletal dynamics. The cell-based approach is orthogonal to direct detection of circulating amyloid and tau, and these exploratory findings support further evaluation of AD-iCAP in prospective studies for combinatorial diagnostics and patient stratification for clinical trials.

title: Associations between early antidepressant exposure, affective states, and subjective sleep quality among euthymic depressive-onset bipolar patients: a cross-sectional parallel mediation analysis
abstract: Bipolar Disorder (BD) is often misdiagnosed as major depressive disorder, leading to prolonged antidepressant use during the early stages. Antidepressant treatment has shown significant effects on affective states and sleep. However, the relationship between early antidepressant use, affective states, and sleep quality has yet to be explored in the BD population. A cross-sectional, single-blind study was conducted in Tianjin Anding Hospital between 1st September 2020 and 30th May 2023. BD patients were categorized into antidepressant treatment (AT) and non-antidepressant treatment (NT) groups based on whether they received early-stage systematic antidepressant treatment. Affective states and subjective sleep quality were measured using the Positive and Negative Affect Schedule (PANAS) and Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI), respectively. Spearman’s correlation examined associations among antidepressant use, affective states, and sleep; mediation effects of affective states were analyzed using a bootstrap method. A total of 124 participants were included. Descriptive statistics showed that the AT group had higher PSQI scores than the NT group (Z = − 5.414, p < 0.001). Preliminary correlation analysis revealed positive correlations between systematic antidepressant use and both scores of PSQI (r = 0.488, p < 0.001) and negative affect (NA) (r = 0.216, p = 0.016). Mediation analysis showed positive correlations between early antidepressant use and scores of PSQI (β = 0.8035, p < 0.001) and NA (β = 0.3804, p = 0.0297), while positive affect scores were negatively correlated with PSQI scores (β = − 0.1968, p = 0.0229). The total effect of antidepressant use on sleep quality was significant (95% bootstrap CI = 1.2940, 3.0595). The indirect effect of early antidepressant use on sleep quality through affective states was not significant (95% bootstrap CI = − 0.2190, 0.3602), but the direct effect was significant (95% bootstrap CI = 1.2467, 3.0220). Early systematic antidepressant use in the cohort is associated with poor subjective sleep quality and higher levels of NA, even in the euthymic phase, emphasizing the need for cautious early use of antidepressants in treating BD and the importance of early diagnosis.

title: Are intellectual and developmental disabilities and mental illnesses associated with poorer educational outcomes? Evidence from India’s National Sample Survey
abstract: Globally, one in eight people experiences mental illness, yet its intersection with education remains under-explored in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs). This study uses nationally representative data from the 76th round of the National Sample Survey (2018) for India to examine how intellectual and developmental (IDD) disability and mental illness—treated as distinct categories—are associated with low educational attainments. Employing a generalised ordered logit model, we found that IDDs were associated with a 71.3% probability of receiving no formal education, while the corresponding risk for respondents with mental illness was 48.3%. Females with mental illness were 18.7% points more likely than males to receive no formal education among mentally ill respondents. Economic affluence reduces the gender gap, but it persists even in the richest quintile among mentally ill respondents. These findings highlight that income-based solutions are insufficient and underscore the need for gender-sensitive mental health and education policies in LMICs to attain Sustainable Development Goals related to mental health, education, gender, and income inequality.

title: An effective and deep learning model to predict Alzheimer’s disease at an early stage from audio data
abstract: A leading cause of dementia, called Alzheimer’s disease (AD), poses a challenge to both patients and their families in multiple ways. Thus, the early identification of AD using symptoms is essential to provide effective treatment and medication. Traditional methods, including scale tests, electroencephalograms, magnetic resonance imaging, and audio analysis, offer a scalable approach for the automatic detection of AD and are gaining popularity among researchers. DL-based approaches are mainly applied to audio analysis for AD and have reached better results. This study proposes an optimized deep learning (DL) model for AD prediction from audio data by employing an effective embedding mechanism. Initially, the collected audio data from the DementiaBank Pitt Corpus dataset undergoes preprocessing to enhance the dataset’s quality, which includes noise filtering using the Weiner filter and then data augmentation to strengthen the dataset’s diversity. After that, the Dilated Convoluted Wav2vec (DCWav2vec) extracts useful pre-processed data features. Finally, the AD classification is performed using the Lyrebird Optimized Gated Recurrent Unit (LOGRU) method, in which the hyperparameters are optimally selected using the Latin hypercube with non-convergence factor centered Lyrebird optimization (LNLBO) algorithm. The experimental results showed that our model can detect AD with an average accuracy of 97.59% and a specificity of 97.57%, which is higher than that of existing models. Finally, this research study concludes that audio-based methods have the potential to be a promising tool for the early detection of dementia.

title: Somatic symptoms in cisgender men, transgender men, and gender-diverse individuals assigned male at birth: a Swiss Nationwide Study
abstract: Abstract Somatic symptoms are highly prevalent and constitute a major public health concern. Sociodemographic factors associated with these symptoms, particularly among cisgender men, transgender men, and gender-diverse individuals, remain insufficiently explored in Switzerland. We analyzed data from the Swiss Health Survey 2022, a nationally representative cross-sectional study. The sample included cisgender men, transgender men (i.e., assigned female at birth and identifying as men), and gender-diverse assigned male at birth (AMAB) individuals (i.e., assigned male at birth and currently identifying as nonbinary or another gender). Somatic symptom load was assessed by combining common somatic complaints including gastrointestinal issues, pain, palpitations, and weakness and subsequently dichotomized into lower vs. severe symptom burden. Sleep problems were measured by difficulties falling asleep, restless sleep, repeated awakenings, and early-morning awakening and categorized into no/few vs. moderate/severe sleep problems for subsequent analyses. Energy and vitality were assessed using the Short Form 36 Health Survey (SF-36) Vitality (VT) subscale, capturing fatigue, tiredness, and overall vitality over the past four weeks and were analyzed as a continuous outcome. Data were analyzed using IBM SPSS Statistics©. Two binary logistic regression analyses were conducted for symptom load and sleep problems, respectively, and one linear regression analysis was performed for vitality as a continuous outcome. To account for the complex survey design, all analyses incorporated survey weights and canton as the stratification variable using design-based (complex samples) procedures. The analytical sample comprised 8,699 individuals (unweighted), representing an estimated population of 3,505,801 after applying survey weights. Compared with cisgender men, gender-diverse AMAB individuals showed higher odds of severe somatic symptom load (OR = 7.82, 95% CI [2.50; 24.45]), whereas transgender men did not differ significantly on this outcome (OR = 1.22, 95% CI [0.39; 3.76]). Both groups showed higher odds of sleep problems (transgender men: OR = 4.66, 95% CI [1.64; 13.25]; gender-diverse AMAB individuals: OR = 3.87, 95% CI [1.21; 12.30]) and lower vitality scores (B=-13.70, 95% CI [-20.04; -7.35]; B=-14.70, 95% CI [-25.93; -3.47], respectively). These estimates rest on small unweighted subgroups (35 transgender men, 16 gender-diverse AMAB individuals), are correspondingly imprecise, and should be read as exploratory. Additional factors associated with poorer outcomes included non-heterosexual orientation, nonemployable status, migration background, and residence in French- or Italian-speaking regions. Older age (65 + years) was associated with lower odds of severe somatic symptom load (OR = 0.71, 95% CI [0.53; 0.96]) but higher odds of sleep problems (OR = 1.35, 95% CI [1.08; 1.70]) and higher vitality scores (B = 8.89, 95% CI [6.83; 10.95]). Factors associated with somatic symptom load, sleep problems, and vitality showed both shared and outcome-specific patterns. Gender identity was associated with poorer sleep and lower vitality in transgender men and gender-diverse AMAB individuals compared with cisgender men, whereas higher somatic symptom load was found only in gender-diverse AMAB individuals. Given the small unweighted subgroup sizes and the resulting imprecision of the estimates, these findings should be interpreted cautiously and considered exploratory and hypothesis-generating rather than confirmatory. These preliminary findings highlight the importance of differentiating gender identities and adopting a gender-sensitive perspective in research and healthcare to better identify vulnerable groups and inform targeted interventions.

title: Machine learning-based multiclass classification of cognitive decline using ACE-III assessment data: a comparative study with SHAP explainability
abstract: Abstract Dementia and its earlier stages mild cognitive impairment (MCI) and subjective cognitive decline (SCD) are increasingly common, yet automated tools that distinguish all four cognitive states simultaneously remain rare. Most published models address a simpler binary problem; the four-class case, which is what clinicians actually face, has attracted far less attention. We developed and benchmarked twelve machine learning classifiers spanning linear, kernel-based, tree-based, boosting, probabilistic, distance-based, and ensemble meta-learning paradigms for four-class cognitive stratification (Cognitively Normal, SCD, MCI, Dementia) using ACE-III assessment-derived clinical and demographic data ( n = 140, 28 features). Class imbalance was mitigated through pipeline-integrated Synthetic Minority Over-sampling Technique (SMOTE), with model evaluation conducted via stratified five-fold cross-validation. All performance metrics (accuracy, macro F1-score, ROC-AUC, balanced accuracy, Cohen’s Kappa, Matthews Correlation Coefficient) were computed across folds and reported as mean ± standard deviation. SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) analysis was employed to quantify global and local feature contributions across all model types. LightGBM achieved the highest macro F1-score (0.723 ± 0.114), ROC-AUC (0.944 ± 0.030), and Cohen’s Kappa (0.729 ± 0.138) among the twelve classifiers, with a balanced accuracy of 0.716 ± 0.121. Voting Classifier attained a near-identical balanced accuracy (0.716 ± 0.068) and the highest single-model MCC (0.734 ± 0.091), closely matching LightGBM’s own MCC (0.733 ± 0.139), and ranked second by macro F1-score (0.714 ± 0.058). k-NN and SVM ranked third and fourth by macro F1-score (0.640 ± 0.136 and 0.631 ± 0.095, respectively), while Gaussian Naïve Bayes performed least favourably (F1: 0.480 ± 0.143). A paired t-test found LightGBM’s macro F1-score advantage statistically significant against one of the eleven remaining classifiers, Logistic Regression (t = 6.783, p = 0.0025, Holm-adjusted p = 0.0271), while differences from the other ten classifiers — including its closest competitors, Voting Classifier, k-NN, and Extra Trees — did not reach significance at this sample size. SHAP analysis identified age, health-condition status, educational attainment, depression, blood pressure, and family history of MCI/Alzheimer’s disease as the most consistently influential predictors across model types. LightGBM classifier trained on Egyptian Arabic ACE-III data classifies patients into four cognitive categories with accuracy that is promising for pre-screening or triage role, though external validation on independent cohorts is needed before any claim of clinical utility can be made, and SHAP makes its reasoning transparent. The framework requires no specialist equipment and runs on data already collected in routine Egyptian encounters, making primary care deployment in Egypt and the MENA region practical pending that validation.

title: Sexual function problems, sexual distress, and operationally defined female sexual dysfunction among women with infertility in southern Iran: a cross-sectional study
abstract: Infertility can negatively affect women’s sexual health. However, low sexual function and sexual distress are different concepts and should not be used interchangeably. This study aimed to estimate the prevalence of low sexual function, sexual distress, and operationally defined female sexual dysfunction (FSD) among women with infertility in southern Iran, and to examine their associations with selected sociodemographic and infertility-related characteristics. In this cross-sectional study, 455 women attending an infertility center in Bandar Abbas, southern Iran, were recruited by simple random sampling from November 2023 to September 2024. Sexual function and sexual distress were assessed using the Female Sexual Function Index (FSFI) and the Female Sexual Distress Scale-Revised (FSDS-R), respectively. Low sexual function was defined as FSFI ≤ 26.55, sexual distress as FSDS- R ≥ 11, and operationally defined FSD as the concurrent presence of both conditions. Three separate multivariable logistic regression models were fitted for low sexual function, sexual distress, and FSD. The prevalence of low sexual function, sexual distress, and FSD was 92.1%, 33.8%, and 31.6%, respectively. In the revised multivariable models, longer infertility duration was associated with higher odds of sexual distress and FSD. Compared with an infertility duration of 1 to 5 years, a duration of 16 to 25 years was associated with higher, but imprecisely estimated, odds of sexual distress (adjusted OR = 3.14, 95% CI: 1.40 to 7.09; p = 0.006) and FSD (adjusted OR = 3.07, 95% CI: 1.36 to 6.91; p = 0.007). Moderate economic status was associated with lower odds of FSD than unfavorable economic status (adjusted OR = 0.57, 95% CI: 0.35 to 0.91; p = 0.018). Estimates from the exploratory low-sexual-function model were less precise and should be interpreted cautiously because the outcome distribution was markedly imbalanced. Among women receiving infertility care in southern Iran, low sexual function was highly prevalent, whereas about one-third experienced sexual distress or met the combined criteria for FSD. Longer infertility duration was associated with higher odds of sexual distress and FSD. These findings support the importance of assessing both sexual function and sexual distress in infertility care, and of interpreting combined questionnaire-based definitions cautiously in the absence of a formal clinical diagnosis.

title: Interpretable attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder diagnosis from functional magnetic resonance imaging via hybrid convolutional neural network–transformer learning and multi-level graph-based comprehensibility
abstract: Attention-Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) is a disorder about the brain development with various changes in the brain structure, involving constant diagnosis using predictable neuroimaging analysis. Current deep learning methods appear to show promising performance in computerized ADHD classification using magnetic resonance imaging (MRI); however, their applicability is restricted due to ambiguity. The proposed study is an interpretable hybrid deep learning model for ADHD recognition using fMRI. It uses a three-dimensional Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) to map brain structures and a transformer encoder to analyse transformer modules. At the voxel level, 3D Grad-CAM + + limits the characteristic feature support for ADHD classification. At the interpretative level, cross-layer attention aggregation creates reliable attention patterns during transformer layers, streamlining the identification of related brain structures. A brain connectivity graph is created by extracting region-specific features using a neuroanatomical atlas, and this graph is then inspected using a Graph Neural Network (GNN). GNNExplainer revealed complex brain subnetworks and interregional interactions related to ADHD. Experiments conducted on the ADHD-200 dataset demonstrated that the proposed hybrid framework exceeded the CNN-only and Transformer-only baselines in terms of accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, and AUC. These results show that the proposed approach has better diagnostic efficacy while providing substantial benefits, progressing the feasibility of deep-learning-based ADHD diagnosis from MRI.

title: Retinal reflectance spectra measured using hyperspectral imaging are associated with prevalent dementia in a general older Japanese population
abstract: Advances in retinal hyperspectral imaging demonstrate its potential usefulness in neurodegenerative disorders; however, community-based evidence is lacking. We examined associations between retinal reflectance spectra and prevalent dementia in 857 Hisayama Study residents aged ≥ 65 years who underwent eye and dementia examinations in 2022–2023. Retinal relative reflectance spectra were measured in four retinal regions using hyperspectral imaging; ganglion cell-inner plexiform layer (GC-IPL) thickness was assessed using optical coherence tomography (OCT). Principal component analysis (PCA) was performed on Z-standardized reflectance values for each retinal region and all four regions combined. PCA-derived scores were constructed as the linear predictor from logistic regression models including the first four principal components, with higher scores indicating lower overall reflectance. Higher PCA-derived scores were significantly associated with higher odds of prevalent dementia in all regions, strongest in inferotemporal region (odds ratio [OR], 2.21; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.46–3.35) and combined regions (OR, 2.20; 95% CI, 1.42–3.40). After internal validation, the shrinkage-adjusted ORs were 2.31 and 2.52, and C-statistics were 0.707 and 0.688, respectively. Coexisting high PCA-derived scores and GC-IPL thinning further had higher odds of prevalent dementia in combined regions (OR, 3.87) and inferotemporal region (OR, 6.98). Thus, hyperspectral imaging, particularly when considered alongside OCT, may capture retinal alterations associated with dementia in older adults.

title: Associations of physical function and multimorbidity with cognitive impairment in community-dwelling Chinese octogenarians
abstract: China’s rapidly aging population has intensified concerns about cognitive impairment and chronic disease burdens among older adults. Despite this, research on the interplay between physical function, multimorbidity, and their associations with cognitive impairment in community-dwelling octogenarians remains limited. This study investigates the associations between physical function, chronic disease prevalence, and cognitive impairment among home-dwelling adults aged ≥ 80 years in China, with a focus on demographic and clinical predictors of cognitive decline. A cross-sectional analysis of 13,027 octogenarians assessed physical function using the Barthel Index (BI) and cognitive status via the Mini-Cog. Logistic regression models evaluated the impact of demographic factors (age, gender, occupation), chronic diseases (hypertension, stroke), and psychosocial factors (aggression, depression) on cognitive impairment severity. Of the participants, 37.88% exhibited high functional independence (BI = 100). Cognitive impairment was significantly influenced by age, gender, and multimorbidity ( p < 0.01). Depression (OR 11.335; 95% CI 8.853–14.514) and aggression (OR 1.93; 95% CI 1.161–3.217) were strongly associated with cognitive impairment severity. Hypertension was moderately correlated with mild cognitive impairment (OR 1.495; 95% CI 1.285–1.739), while stroke tripled the odds of mild-to-moderate cognitive impairment (OR 3.301; 95% CI 2.131–5.113). Reduced self-care ability was associated with nearly fourfold higher odds of cognitive impairment ( p < 0.01). Age, occupation, and lifestyle factors synergistically are associated with chronic disease burden and cognitive impairment in China’s oldest-old population. These findings underscore the urgency of personalized healthcare strategies to preserve independence and mitigate cognitive decline in high-risk octogenarians.

title: Multimodal patch-based deep learning for early Alzheimer’s disease classification using MRI and PET
abstract: Alzheimer’s disease (AD) is a neurodegenerative condition in which detection of pathological changes in the early stages, especially during the mild cognitive impairment (MCI) phase, is key for early diagnosis and treatment of the disease. While MRI gives a structural view of the brain, FDG-PET is complementary in providing a view of functional and metabolic changes in the brain due to neurodegeneration. In this study, we propose a multimodal patch-based deep learning framework for classification of AD, MCI, and cognitively normal (NC) patients based on MRI and FDG-PET data pairs. Data consisted of 168 patients from the Alzheimer’s Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) database, which include 58 AD, 54 MCI, and 56 NC patients. T1-weighted MRI and FDG-PET volumes were preprocessed and registered to a common spatial space, followed by extraction of non-overlapping 3-D patches. We then extracted structural and functional features using two 3D convolutional neural networks (3D-CNNs), and finally multimodal fusion of features was performed. In order to increase the robustness of the final prediction results, a stacking-based ensemble algorithm employing a 1D-CNN meta-learner was utilized for fusing the base model prediction outputs. The performance of the models was evaluated by subject-level five-fold cross-validation, while accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, and AUC were selected as evaluation criteria. The proposed full framework reached the average accuracies of 97.50% ± 2.40%, 99.00% ± 1.90%, and 96.00% ± 2.10% for NC vs. MCI, AD vs. NC, and AD vs. MCI diagnosis, respectively, achieving corresponding AUCs of 0.983, 0.996, and 0.973. Ablation analysis also proved that the patch-based representation, multimodal feature fusion, and stacking helped achieve the desired classification performance, since the full framework significantly outperformed all the ablated configurations ( p < 0.01). Based on the obtained results, it is possible to claim that combining the localized structural and metabolic features provided by the MRI and FDG-PET scans within the framework of the patch-based 3D deep learning algorithm can help effectively discriminate between AD, MCI, and cognitively normal subjects. Additional validation is necessary before applying the framework in clinical practice.

title: Latent profiles of mental health literacy and associated factors among older adults with cataracts
abstract: Abstract Mental health literacy may shape how older adults with cataracts recognize psychological distress and seek support, but variation within this population remains poorly understood. This cross-sectional study surveyed 209 hospitalized adults aged 60 years or older with cataracts using validated measures of mental health literacy, anxiety, perceived social support and sleep quality. Latent profile analysis identified three mental health literacy profiles: low-MHL/negative-attitude (16.7%), limited-recognition/moderate-attitude (33.5%) and high-MHL (49.8%). Multinomial logistic regression showed that diagnosis duration, anxiety level, living arrangement and primary caregiver were associated with profile membership. These findings highlight different patterns of recognition and attitudes within this hospitalized sample. They support examining these dimensions separately in nursing assessment research. Independent validation is required before using the profiles to guide nursing assessment or select educational support.

title: An uncertainty-aware multimodal deep learning framework for Alzheimer’s disease classification using MRI and electronic health records
abstract: Despite significant advances in artificial intelligence, achieving early and accurate diagnosis of Alzheimer’s disease (AD) remains a challenging task due to the complexity, heterogeneity, noise, and uncertainty inherent in neurological and clinical data. Conventional machine learning and deep learning models generally rely on deterministic decision boundaries, which limits their ability to manage diagnostic uncertainty and ambiguous cases, particularly during the early Mild Cognitive Impairment (MCI) stage. This study presents a reinforcement learning–optimized fuzzy deep learning framework for uncertainty-aware prediction of AD. The proposed framework integrates convolutional neural networks (CNN) and bidirectional long short-term memory (BiLSTM) networks to learn comprehensive multimodal representations by extracting spatial features from MRI images and temporal patterns from electronic health record (EHR) data. The learned features are further processed through a fuzzy inference system, enabling soft classification and explicit modelling of uncertainty in diagnostic decisions. Additionally, a reinforcement learning (RL)-based optimization mechanism is introduced to adaptively optimize classification parameters and fuzzy membership functions, thereby enhancing model robustness, generalization capability, and predictive performance. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed framework achieves superior performance compared with conventional machine learning and deep learning approaches, attaining an accuracy of 98.9%, precision of 98.7%, recall of 98.8%, F1-score of 98.8%, and an AUC of 0.99. In contrast, the baseline CNN–BiLSTM model achieved 96.4% accuracy and an AUC of 0.97. Statistical evaluation using the DeLong test confirmed that the performance improvement was significant ( p < 0.05). These findings indicate that the proposed uncertainty-aware framework provides a reliable and effective computational approach for early AD diagnosis and clinical decision support.

title: Higher plasma oleic acid is associated with slower progression from mild cognitive impairment to Alzheimer’s disease in men and women
abstract: The contribution of sex differences in lipid metabolism to the pathophysiology of Alzheimer’s disease (AD) remains under Investigation. This study aimed to investigate sex-stratified associations of fatty acid (FA) profiles in cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) and plasma across the AD continuum, and their associations with AD pathology and progression. FA profiles were analyzed in 198 CSF and 286 plasma samples from AD, mild cognitive impairment (MCI), and control subjects using GC-FID. The MCI subjects were followed up for 58 (± 12.5) months. Analysis of FA profiles of control subjects revealed minor sex differences in both CSF and plasma biofluids. In men, a higher CSF anti-inflammatory index was associated with lower odds of AD than MCI (OR = 0.025), whereas higher CSF α-linolenic acid (C18:3n-3) levels were associated with higher odds of AD (OR = 2.826). In women, higher CSF levels of palmitoleic acid (C16:1n-7) were associated with lower odds of amyloid-β (Aβ) positivity (OR = 0.500). Higher plasma oleic acid (C18:1n-9) levels were associated with lower odds of MCI-to-AD progression in men (OR = 0.666) and a longer time to progression in women (HR = 0.404). Our results suggest that higher plasma oleic acid levels were associated with slower disease progression in both men and women, whereas higher CSF anti-inflammatory index and α-linolenic acid were associated with AD diagnosis in men. These findings may reflect differences in lipid metabolism associated with AD across men and women, although reverse causation and residual confounding cannot be excluded.
